questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the right coronary artery?

options.A: It’s diameter is less than left coronary artery
options.B: It arises from the right aortic sinus
options.C: It gives rise to circumflex coronary branch
options.D: Right conal artery is it’s first branch

explanation.text: It gives rise to the circumflex coronary branch. This statement is false. The right coronary artery does not typically give rise to the circumflex coronary branch. The circumflex branch is a branch

of the left coronary artery. It wraps around the left side of the heart and supplies blood to the left atrium and portions of the left ventricle. Incorrect Options: Option A - Its diameter is less than the left coronary artery. This statement is generally true.Left coronary artery (LCA) typically has a slightly larger diameter than the the right coronary artery (RCA) Option B - It arises from the anterior aortic sinus. This statement is true.

The right coronary artery originates from the right aortic sinus, which is one of the three aortic sinuses located at the base of the aorta. Option D - Right conal artery is its first branch. This statement is true. The right conal artery is indeed the first branch of the right coronary artery.

questions.question: Which of the following veins drain directly into the brachiocephalic vein?

explanation.text: The left superior intercostal vein collects blood from the 2nd and 3rd posterior intercostal veins on the left side of the body and typically directs this blood flow into the left brachiocephalic vein. Incorrect Options: Option A: Hemiazygous vein: Instead of directly connecting to the brachiocephalic vein, it usually joins with the azygous vein, which then empties into the superior vena cava.

Option B: Superior thyroid veins: The superior and middle thyroid veins drain the thyroid gland, flowing into the internal jugular vein rather than directly into the brachiocephalic vein. Option C: Right superior intercostal vein: The right superior intercostal vein drains upper right intercostal spaces, usually joining the azygous vein before reaching the superior vena cava, rather than directly connecting to the brachiocephalic vein.

questions.question: What is the most prominent indication of breast cancer among the options provided?

explanation.text: Peau d'orange refers to the appearance of the breast skin that resembles the texture of an orange peel. It is caused by the infiltration and thickening of the breast skin due to underlying breast cancer. This condition is characterized by dimpling, puckering, or indentation of the skin, giving it a pebbled or orange peel-like appearance.

It occurs due to the obstruction or invasion of lymphatic vessels by cancer cells, resulting in lymphatic congestion and edema. Incorrect Options:: Option B - Nipple retraction: Nipple retraction or inversion can be a sign of breast cancer, but it is not the most conspicuous sign.

Option C - Puckering: Puckering or dimpling of the breast skin can be a sign of breast cancer, but it is not the most conspicuous sign.. Option D - Both nipple retraction and puckering: Nipple retraction and puckering can signal breast cancer, but the most noticeable sign is often peau d'orange.

questions.question: Which artery does not provide blood supply to the corresponding area of the dura mater among the following options?

options.A: Middle meningeal artery – anterior cranial fossa
options.B: Accessory meningeal branch of maxillary artery – middle cranial fossa
options.C: Meningeal branch of internal carotid artery – posterior cranial fossa
options.D: Meningeal branch of anterior and posterior ethmoid artery – anterior cranial fossa

explanation.text: Meningeal branch of the internal carotid artery – posterior cranial fossa: The internal carotid artery primarily supplies the

brain with blood, but it does not directly supply the dura mater in the posterior cranial fossa. Instead, the posterior cranial fossa's dura mater is mainly supplied by branches of the vertebral arteries, including the posterior meningeal arteries.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Middle meningeal artery – anterior cranial fossa: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery and supplies the dura mater in the anterior cranial fossa, including the frontal and parietal regions.

Option B - Accessory meningeal branch of the maxillary artery – middle cranial fossa: The accessory meningeal branch of the maxillary artery supplies the dura mater in the middle cranial fossa, which includes the temporal and sphenoid regions.

Option D - Meningeal branch of anterior and posterior ethmoid artery – anterior cranial fossa: The meningeal branches of the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries supply the dura mater in the anterior cranial fossa, specifically the ethmoid and frontal regions.

questions.question: Which of the following does not supply the marked structure?

explanation.text: The diagonal artery does not supply the marked structure (right ventricle). The diagonal artery is a branch of the left anterior descending artery and primarily supplies the left ventricle and the anterior walls of the heart. Incorrect Option: Option A - The right coronary artery supplies blood to the right ventricle, which is the marked structure.

It's one of the main arteries responsible for nourishing the right side of the heart.. Option B - The anterior interventricular artery, a branch of the left coronary artery, supplies blood to the interventricular septum and front walls of both ventricles, including the right ventricle. Option C - The marginal artery, a branch of the right coronary artery, supplies blood to the right ventricle.
It runs along the heart's right border, providing blood to the right ventricle's lateral wall.

questions.question: Marked structure is derived from the ?

explanation.text: The endocardial cushions play a crucial role in the development of the heart's septa and valves. They contribute to the formation of various structures, including the atrial septum, ventricular septum, and the atrioventricular (AV) valves. Therefore, it is correct to say that the marked structure is derived from the endocardial cushions.

Incorrect Option: Option B - Septum primum: During embryonic development, the septum primum grows downward from the roof of the primitive atrium but doesn't directly form the marked structure. Option C - Left venous valve: The left venous valve regulates blood flow from the coronary sinus in the right atrium but doesn't contribute to the marked structure's formation.
Option D - Bulbous venosus: The bulbous venosus, part of the embryonic heart tube, helps form the right ventricle but doesn't directly create the marked structure.

questions.question: The region marked corresponds to the surface marking for which of the following structures:-

explanation.text: The marked region corresponds to the surface marking for the right atrium, which aligns with the right sternal border. Incorrect Option: Option A - The thoracic duct in the posterior mediastinum drains lymph from the lower and left upper body into the venous system but isn't represented by the marked region on the image. Option C - Inferomedial bronchopulmonary segments are specific regions within the lungs.

They are not related to the region marked on the image, which is external to the lungs. Option D - The hilum is where blood vessels, nerves, and bronchi enter or exit an organ, like the hila of the lungs. However, the marked region on the image isn't the hilum.

questions.question: Sternum is attached to scapula via?

explanation.text: Clavicle: The clavicle is a bone that connects the sternum (specifically the manubrium) to the scapula. It forms the acromioclavicular joint with the scapula, providing a direct attachment between the sternum and the scapula. This makes option B correct. Incorrect Options: Option A - Manubrium: The manubrium is the top portion of the sternum and forms the sternoclavicular joint with the clavicle.

However, it doesn't directly connect to the scapula. Option C - First rib: The first rib, attaching to the sternum at the sternocostal joint, isn't directly involved in connecting the sternum to the scapula. Option D - Second rib: The second rib, like the first rib, attaches to the sternum at the sternocostal joint, but it isn't directly linked to the scapula.

questions.question: Mediastinal surface of the right lung is related to? A. The Azygos vein B. The Right Lymphatic Duct C. The Aorta D. The Trachea

explanation.text: The Azygos vein: The azygos vein is a major vein that drains blood from the posterior part of the thoracic wall into the superior vena cava. It does run along the mediastinal surface of the right lung, making option A correct. Incorrect Options: Option B - Lymphatic vessel that drains lymph from the upper right quadrant of the body.

Option C - While the aortais located in the mediastinum, it is positioned more towards the left side rather than the mediastinal surface of the right lung. Option D - The trachea travels down the center of the thoracic cavity, behind the mediastinal surface of both lungs. Although it's close to the mediastinal surface of the right lung, it's not directly connected to it.

questions.question: The structure not passing through the aortic opening of the diaphragm is:

explanation.text: The aortic opening of the diaphragm, also known as the aortic hiatus, is an opening in the diaphragm through which structures pass between the thoracic and abdominal cavities. It is located at the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra. The vagal trunk comes through an esophageal opening at 10th thoracic vertebra.

Incorrect Options Option A - Aorta: The aorta, the largest artery in the body, passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm.. Option B - Azygous vein: The azygous vein, an important venous channel in the thorax, ascends on the right side of the vertebral column and passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm.
Option C - Thoracic duct: The thoracic duct, the main lymphatic vessel in the body, also passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Sibson's fascia is not correct?

options.A: Attached to the inner border of 2 nd rib
options.C: Not a part of scalenus minimus muscle

explanation.text: Sibson's fascia attaches to the inner border of the 1st rib and covers the apical part of the lung. Sibson's fascia, also known as the suprapleural membrane, is a thin layer of connective tissue located at the apex of the lung. Incorrect Options: Option B - Covers apical part of the lung: This statement is correct. Sibson's fascia covers the apical part of the lung and forms a protective layer over the lung apex.

Option C - Not a part of scalenus minimus muscle: This statement is correct. The scalenus minimus muscle is a small muscle found in some individuals near the apex of the lung, but it is not directly associated with Sibson's fascia. Option D - Vessels pass above the fascia: This statement is correct. Sibson's fascia shields the lung apex from blood vessels like the subclavian vessels and brachiocephalic veins.

questions.question: The joint between the attachment of the 8 th and 9 th rib to the 7 th rib is a:

explanation.text: The joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib to the 7th rib is classified as a synovial joint. Synovial joints are characterized by the presence of a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid, which allows for smooth movement between the articulating surfaces.

Incorrect Options: Option A - Fibrocartilaginous joint: Fibrocartilaginous joints, like intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis, provide stability with limited movement due to fibrocartilage between bones.. Option B - Symphyseal joint: Symphyseal joints, featuring hyaline and fibrocartilage, allow limited movement and are seen in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs.

Option D - Fibrous joint: Fibrous joints, like skull sutures, typically allow minimal movement due to fibrous connective tissue. However, the joint between the 8th and 9th rib attachment to the 7th rib permits movement and isn't solely fibrous.

questions.question: After a fall from a height with his hand outstretched, a man is brought to the emergency department. An X-ray reveals a fracture in the clavicle. Which specific region of the clavicle is the most likely to be fractured?

explanation.text: The junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd of the clavicle. This is the most common site of clavicular fracture, accounting for approximately 80% of all clavicular fractures. This area is also known as the "junction" or "transition zone" because it is where the clavicle changes from a thicker, more rounded bone to a thinner, flatter bone.

Incorrect Options: Option B - Junction of medial 1/3rd and lateral 2/3rd: Clavicular fractures at this junction are rare due to its thickness and strength, needing considerable force to cause a fracture Option C - Junction of middle 1/3rd and medial 1/3rd: Fractures at the middle 1/3rd and medial 1/3rd junction of the clavicle are uncommon due to its thinner and more flexible nature.
Option D - Middle of the clavicle: Mid-clavicular fractures are uncommon and typically result from direct trauma or a fall onto the shoulder, rather than a fall onto an outstretched hand.

questions.question: The inferior scapular angle is at which vertebrae level?

explanation.text: The superior scapular angle is located at T2, while the inferior scapular angle is situated at T7. Incorrect Options: A, C, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: In the given section of the heart, match the marked (A,B,C&D) structures. Musculi pectinate Anterior papillary muscle of left ventricle Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle Anterior leaflet of mitral valve membranous part of ventricular septum

explanation.text: A - Membranous part of ventricular septum B - Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle C - Anterior papillary muscle of left ventricle D - Musculi pectinate Incorrect Options - A, B & D are incorrect answer

questions.question: The image shows the cross-section of the abdominal cavity. Identify the structure marked ‘A.’

explanation.text: The diagram focuses on the posterior mediastinum, and the marked structure is descending aorta. The round structure just in front of the vertebral column is descending aorta, slightly towards the left. The descending aorta is located posterior to the diaphragm, in the midline of the body. It is a continuation of the thoracic aorta and descends along the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum before entering the abdominal cavity.

In the abdominal cavity, it descends along the posterior wall, slightly to the left of the midline, and gives off branches to the abdominal organs. Incorrect Options: Option B - Superior vena cava: The superior vena cava, found in the superior mediastinum, enters the right atrium of the heart. It is not visible in abdominal cavity cross-sections.

Option C - Inferior vena cava: The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from the posterior mediastinum, traveling along the back of the abdominal wall to the right of the midline, collecting blood from the lower body and abdominal organs.

Option D - Ascending aorta: The ascending aorta begins at the left ventricle, ascends to the superior mediastinum, and branches into the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery.

questions.question: A newborn presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. An abdominal X-ray shows signs of bowel obstruction. Intraoperatively, the surgeon finds multiple fibrous bands with the cecum on the left side and the small intestine on the right side. What is the most likely underlying anomaly?

explanation.text: Nonrotation of the midgut refers to a congenital anomaly where the midgut only completes the first 90° of the normal 270° counterclockwise rotation, leaving the midgut improperly positioned within the abdomen. This leads to abnormal positioning of the small intestine on the right and the colon on the left, predisposing the infant to volvulus and obstruction, as seen in this case.

The bilious vomiting and abdominal distension are typical presentations of midgut volvulus. Types of malrotation Characteristic Non-Rotation Incomplete Rotation Reverse Rotation Features Failure of normal 270° counterclockwise rotation. Only the first 90° rotation occurs. Small intestine is on the right side and large intestine on the left. Incomplete rotation. Large intestine passes behind the duodenum and the superior mesenteric artery (SMA).

SMA compresses the duodenum. Intestines rotate 90° clockwise instead of counterclockwise. Large intestine returns earlier and lies behind the duodenum and SMA. Small intestine misplaced anteriorly. Clinical Presentation Abdominal distension Bilious vomiting (if volvulus occurs) Absent IC junction in RIF IC junction may be midline, below the pylorus.

Bilious vomiting Abdominal pain and distension Features of duodenal obstruction (due to SMA compression). Bilious vomiting Failure to thrive Symptoms of bowel obstruction Possible shock if volvulus is present. Complications Volvulus Intestinal obstruction Surgical Management Ladd’s procedure Midgut volvulus with normal rotation (Option D): Midgut
volvulus can still occur even with normal rotation, but it’s not the underlying cause here as the infant has abnormal rotation.

questions.question: A newborn presents with bilious vomiting shortly after birth. X-ray abdomen is taken and is shown below. Further evaluation reveals pancreatic tissue encircling and compressing the second part of the duodenum. Which embryological structure is primarily responsible for this congenital abnormality?

explanation.text: Bilious vomiting, x-ray showing double bubble sign of duodenal obstruction and evaluation indicating presence of pancreatic tissue encircling and compressing the second part of the duodenum is suggestive of Annular pancreas, occurring due to abnormal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud.

Development of pancreas: Origin of Pancreatic Buds & its derivatives Dorsal Pancreatic Bud: located in the dorsal mesentery, forms the upper part of the head, neck, body, and tail of the pancreas. Ventral Pancreatic Bud: Arises near the hepatic bud in the ventral mesentery. Forms the lower part of the head and the uncinate process.

Rotation and Fusion: Rotation of the duodenal loop brings the ventral pancreatic bud to the right side of the duodenum, eventually fusing with the dorsal bud. Except for the tail, the pancreas becomes retroperitoneal after the fusion and rotation. Duct System Formation Main Pancreatic Duct (wirsung): Formed from the distal part of the dorsal duct and proximal part of the ventral duct.

Accessory Pancreatic Duct (santorini): Derived from the proximal portion of the dorsal duct. Papillae Openings The main pancreatic duct opens into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla with the bile duct. The accessory duct opens at the minor duodenal papilla. Exocrine and Endocrine Components Exocrine Pancreas: Derived from endodermal cells that reorganize into acini.
Endocrine Pancreas: The islets of Langerhans develop from cells separating from the duct system. Developmental anomalies of Pancreas 1.

Annular pancreas: The ventral pancreatic bud consists of two components that typically fuse and rotate around the duodenum, positioning below the dorsal bud. (Option B) Sometimes, the right part migrates normally while the left moves in the opposite direction, leading to malformations that can constrict the 2nd part of the duodenum and cause obstruction. 2.

Pancreatic divisum: Failure of fusion of parts of pancreas derived from dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds with each other. This leads to most pancreatic secretions draining through the accessory duct (duct of Santorini) into the minor papilla, which is often smaller and can become obstructed. This incomplete drainage leads to recurrent pancreatitis.

Accessory pancreatic tissue Accessory pancreatic tissue can be found in various locations, including: Stomach wall Duodenum (most common) Meckel’s diverticulum Greater omentum Hilum of the spleen It appears as yellowish, lobulated nodules, typically single and ranging from 1–6 mm in diameter.
Approximately one-third of these nodules contain islets of Langerhans.
**Dorsal pancreatic bud (Option A):** Forms parts of the pancreas (body, neck, and tail), but does not encircle the duodenum and is not involved in annular pancreas formation.
**Hepatic diverticulum (Option C):** Develops into the liver and bile ducts, unrelated to pancreatic development or duodenal obstruction.
**Vitelline duct (Option D):** Related to the yolk sac and conditions like Meckel's diverticulum, not involved in pancreatic or duodenal development.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the peritoneal folds of abdomen?

options.A: The greater omentum attaches to the lesser curvature of the stomach and the duodenum, providing a barrier to infections in the peritoneal cavity.
options.B: The lesser omentum connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the diaphragm and provides support to the liver
options.C: The greater omentum forms a fold between the liver and the diaphragm, providing structural support to the stomach.
options.D: The greater omentum is often used as a free flap in reconstructive surgeries based on gastro-omental vessels in gastrointestinal perforations.

explanation.text: The remarkable capacity of the greater omentum to participate in reparative processes is highlighted by its use as an omental pedicle flap or free flap in reconstructive surgery: it has been used to support closure of gastrointestinal perforations, fill ‘dead space’ after surgical excision of pathology, and cover wound defects. Peritoneum: The peritoneum consists of 2 layers: the superficial parietal layer and the deep visceral layer.
The peritoneal cavity contains the omentum, ligaments, and mesentery. The lesser omentum (or hepatogastric) is attached to the lesser curvature of the stomach and the liver.

The greater omentum (or gastrocolic) hangs from the greater curvature of the stomach and loops down in front of the intestines before curving back upwards to attach to the transverse colon.In effect it is draped in front of the intestines like an apron and may serve as an insulating or protective layer.

questions.question: Match the following with their corresponding dermatomal distribution: Thumb 1) L3 Umblicus 2) L5 Knee 3) C6 Dorsum of foot 4) T10

explanation.text: Thumb 1) C6 Umblicus 2) T10 Knee 3) L3 Dorsum of foot 4) L5 Dermatomes: The sensory fibres in individual spinal and cranial nerves have characteristic, but often overlapping, peripheral (cutaneous) distributions.

As far as the innervation of the body surface is concerned, the area of skin that is supplied by a particular spinal or cranial nerve is referred to as a dermatome, and the areas of skin supplied by named peripheral nerves are often referred to as the peripheral nerve field (or cutaneous nerve distribution) of that nerve.

Nerve root Dermatomal distribution C2 Temple, Forehead, Occiput C3 Entire Neck, Posterior Cheek, Temporal Area, Prolongation forward under Mandible C4 Shoulder Area, Clavicular Area, Upper Scapular Area C5 Deltoid Area, Anterior aspect of entire arm to base of thumb C6 Anterior Arm, Radial side of hand to thumb and index finger C7 Lateral Arm and Forearm to index, long, and ring fingers C8 Medial Arm and forearm to long, ring, and little fingers T1 Medial side of forearm to base of little finger T2 Medial side of upper arm to medial elbow, pectoral and midscapular areas T3-6 Upper Thorax T5-7 Costal Margin T8-12 Abdomen and Lumbar Region L1 Back, over trochanter and groin L2 Back, front of thigh to knee L3 Back, upper buttock, anterior thigh and knee, medial lower leg L4 Medial buttock, latera thigh, medial leg, dorsum of foot, big toe L5 Buttock, posterior and lateral thigh, lateral aspect of leg, dorsum of foot, medial half of sole, first, second, and third toes S1 Buttock, Thigh, and Leg Posterior S2 Same as S1 S3 Groin, medial thigh to knee S4 Perineum, genitals, lower sacrum Clinical significance: A dermatome is an area of skin supplied by sensory neurons that arise from a spinal nerve ganglion.

Symptoms that follow a dermatome (e.g. like pain or a rash) may indicate a pathology that involves the related nerve root. In referred pain, sensory nerve fibers such as that from dermatomes may come together at the same spinal cord level as the general visceral afferent fibers such as that from the heart.

When the general visceral sensory fiber is stimulated, the central nervous system does not clearly discern whether the pain is coming from the body wall or from the viscera, so it perceives the pain as coming from somewhere on the body wall, e.g. left arm/hand pain, jaw pain. So the pain is "referred to" the related dermatomes of the same spinal segment.
